extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (about 95k chars, 1931 lines: front matter, introduction, theory, data and methods, results, conclusion, references, and a pointer to supporting information) in chunks; no section skipped. Metadata hints corrected: full author names taken from the text; year is 2019 (AJPS vol 63 no 1, January 2019; online 2018), not 2018; DOI taken from the text. Appendices A and B are referenced but not in the text file. Paul's annotations: 78 entries in the annotation file (73 Highlight, 5 Ink marks with no covered text). None carries a note (all content fields empty), so every note is empty. paul_markup holds 40 of the 78 entries, chosen for substance in document order; 38 dropped (5 Ink marks, numeric table fragments, and minor duplicate or fragment highlights). extraction.research_question: Why do some bills move forward while others languish? Do interest group endorsements listed in Dear Colleague letters signal bill quality to members of Congress, and does their effect vary across the legislative process?
extraction.theory: Cue-taking under limited information: members with limited time and staff rely on informative signals, and interest group endorsements are cheap, quick cues. H1 and H1a: endorsements from well-connected groups (high eigenvector centrality) are informative, most strongly early in the process. H2 and H2a: the number of endorsing groups matters more later, because it signals broad support and a larger lobbying ground game. Builds on Hall and Deardorff (2006) on lobbying as legislative subsidy and on the Kingdon cue literature.
extraction.data: Electronic Dear Colleague letters sent between House members, 106th to 111th Congresses (1999-2010): 93,967 letters, of which 6,633 bills had letters urging support. Unit is the bill. 27 percent of bills with letters had letters naming interest groups. Endorsing organizations matched to 11,019 organizations in the Amicus Curiae Networks Project plus hand-added names. Outcomes (cosponsors, reported from House committee, passed House) and sponsor data from the Congressional Bills Project. Hot Bills list from the Senate Library. Regression N = 6,597.
extraction.method: Negative binomial regression of the cosponsor count with Congress fixed effects (Table 3; AIC 60,835.04). Logit models for Reported House and Passed House (Table 4), each including cosponsor count as a regressor to capture an indirect path from social power to passage. Standard errors in parentheses; significance stars.
extraction.identification: No causal identification design (no instrument, natural experiment, or bill-level panel). Associational estimates with Congress fixed effects, sponsor and bill controls, and the cosponsor count entered as a downstream regressor. Footnote 11 notes that solicited and group-initiated endorsements cannot be distinguished.
extraction.scope: US House of Representatives only; bills that were the subject of Dear Colleague letters urging support, 1999-2010 (106th to 111th Congresses). Not the full population of introduced bills, and not the Senate, except that robustness on all bills in the 111th Congress is reported in supporting information (not in the text file).

key_findings.finding: Early stage: bills endorsed by well-connected groups attract more cosponsors. Interest Group Social Power has a positive, significant effect on the cosponsor count.
key_findings.numbers: coef 0.055 (SE 0.011), p<.001; predicted cosponsors 33 with unconnected endorsers, 38 with an endorser at centrality 2.51 (Anti-Defamation League), 51 with one at 7.66 (Planned Parenthood)

key_findings.finding: Breadth also raises early cosponsorship: each additional endorsing group adds cosponsors. Matching one moderately connected endorser takes 19 low-centrality groups.
key_findings.numbers: Interest Group Count coef 0.007 (SE 0.001), p<.001; 61 average-centrality endorsers match the 51 predicted for a Planned Parenthood-level endorsement

key_findings.finding: Social power has no significant direct effect on committee reporting or floor passage. The authors describe a single well-connected endorsement as no longer enough late in the process.
key_findings.numbers: Reported House 0.020 (SE 0.031); Passed House -0.035 (SE 0.032); both not significant

key_findings.finding: Breadth matters at the floor stage: the number of endorsing groups significantly predicts House passage but not committee reporting.
key_findings.numbers: Passed House 0.013 (SE 0.004), p<.001; Reported House 0.004 (SE 0.003), not significant

key_findings.finding: Predicted passage probability rises with the number of endorsing groups, though slowly.
key_findings.numbers: predicted probability 0.09 with no endorsements, 0.10 with 10 groups, 0.20 with 75 groups

key_findings.finding: Cosponsorship is an indirect channel from social power to success: cosponsor count predicts both committee reporting and passage.
key_findings.numbers: cosponsors coef 0.002 (SE 0.001), p<.01 for Reported House; 0.004 (SE 0.001), p<.001 for Passed House

key_findings.finding: Hot bills and commemorative bills attract more cosponsors; hot bills and majority-party sponsors are more likely to pass.
key_findings.numbers: hot bill cosponsors coef 0.365 (p<.001), about 15 additional cosponsors; commemorative bills average 78 cosponsors vs 33; Passed House: hot bill 2.428, majority 1.353, both p<.001

key_findings.finding: Network measure example: standardized eigenvector centrality in the amicus curiae network separates well-connected groups from peripheral ones.
key_findings.numbers: NOW 8.2962; NEA 2.6653; AFL-CIO 0.8824; AHA -0.1095; ASA -0.2053 (set as the minimum for groups absent from the network)

key_findings.finding: Sample scale: Dear Colleague letter volume rose sharply over the period.
key_findings.numbers: 31,994 electronic letters in the 111th Congress vs 15,477 in the 109th (up 106.7 percent)

key_findings.finding: Hypothesis pattern: H1a (social power stronger early) and H2a (breadth stronger late) are both supported as stated by the authors.
key_findings.numbers: early social power significant, late social power not; early count significant, late count significant for passage only

key_findings.finding: Conclusion on pluralism: well-connected groups act as early gatekeepers, but broad multi-group support is necessary for passage.

limitations: Endorsements may be solicited by a member's office or initiated by the group; letters do not reveal which (footnote 11, p. 171).

Endorser names were matched to the amicus network and hand-checked; groups absent from the network receive the minimum centrality score, which the authors say understates their influence (footnote 18, p. 173).
The amicus curiae network is used as a proxy for legislative relationships; the authors assume judicial and legislative relationships persist across branches (footnote 15, p. 172).

The analysis is restricted to bills that were the subject of Dear Colleague letters, with opposition letters removed (footnote 14, p. 171). Results for all bills appear only in supporting information.
Hot bill status may be determined after endorsements, which complicates its use as a control (footnote 21, p. 175).
Some letters are purpose-coded from a hand-coded subsample of 4,656 letters (footnote 9, p. 169).
Endorsing groups may not interact with one another, so endorsement lists do not establish coordination (p. 172).
The authors report no systematic per-Congress pattern in the social power and count effects (footnote 22, p. 175).
Associational results; no causal design. The authors describe the results as complex and open new questions (p. 178).
measures: Cosponsors: count of cosponsors in the Congress
Reported House and Passed House: binary outcomes from the Congressional Bills Project
Interest Group Social Power: maximum standardized eigenvector centrality among endorsing groups (amicus curiae network)
Interest Group Count: number of endorsing groups named in the letter
Hot Bills: Senate Library Hot Bills List
Commemorative: Congressional Bills Project designation
Majority, Seniority, Referring Committee, Committee Chair, Ranking Member: sponsor characteristics
Ideological Extremity: absolute difference between first-dimension DW-NOMINATE score and chamber median
Congress fixed effects

paul_markup.text: Why do some pieces of legislation move forward while others languish?

We demonstrate that endorsements from particularly well-connected interest groups are a strong cue for members with limited information early in the legislative process and help grow the list of bill cosponsors.
However, the challenges of doing so with imperfect information have been well documented
Even if they read every bill, members cannot be expected to effectively comprehend the implications of complicated legislative text across a broad array of policy issues.
we identify the interest groups who have endorsed legislation and determine the impact of those endorsements at multiple stages of the legislative process.
By contrast, endorsements from a larger number of groups are better indicators of success later in the process when members need to amass a winning coalition of 218 votes.
devote more of their limited time to fundraising, and have fewer policy staff to support them.
Nowhere in this allocation is time for reviewing legislation introduced by other members or any sort of policy analysis.
As a result, there has been a steady decline in the number of issues Congress can address and its capacity for gathering the information necessary to create policy
Members also rely on interest groups to provide the information they need to make policy decisions.
This information is invaluable to members making voting decisions.
Therefore, a member who is concerned with the approval of a particular interest group will know that a bill is safe to support if it has their endorsement.
Some organizations are more influential than others because they have more resources, greater name recognition, or better connections within the interest group community.
The strength of their relationships with other organizations means they are likely to be well known and in a position to influence other groups.
Members of Congress work to gain the support of stakeholders when they introduce a bill because they expect it will increase the likelihood of success.
Put simply, we expect that when a bill is endorsed by a large number of organizations, the endorsements collectively demonstrate broad support for the policy in question
In addition to signaling that a bill has broad support, endorsements from a large number of organizations translate into a larger ground game.
In what follows, we test whether interest group endorsements play a role in the decision to cosponsor legislation and a bill's success in the House of Representatives.
It can be a crucial factor in building support for legislation, as it is a great way to disseminate what outside organizations are supporting legislation
Fourteen percent of the Dear Colleague letters are from members asking their colleagues to sign a letter to the administration, committee chairs, or congressional leadership.

Members of Congress and their staff have to reach out to organizations they think may be interested in supporting the bill, provide them with the legislative language prior to introduction, wait for the organization to review the bill
If nearly every bill introduced was endorsed by an interest group, the value of those signals would be significantly weakened,
In contrast, the interest groups that have endorsed a bill and are listed together on a Dear Colleague letter may not have any interaction.
As reported by the interest groups themselves, the relationships demonstrated by the cosigning of an amicus curiae brief before the Court do not disappear when those groups are lobbying Congress.
Interest groups with strong connections to other prominent and well-connected organizations have a great deal of social power within the interest group community.
NOW has more social power than the other three organizations, and therefore an endorsement from them is going to send a stronger signal to the average member of Congress than one from the ASA
Interest Group Social Power, which is the largest standardized eigenvector centrality score of the interest groups that have endorsed a bill.
That is, maximum eigenvector centrality allows us to examine whether members are swayed by a single endorsement from a powerful interest group
We expect legislation designated as a hot bill is more likely to pass the House and be signed into law.
The average bill with no endorsements is estimated to have 33 cosponsors.

It takes 61 endorsements from interest groups with no more than the average eigenvector centrality score to match the 51 cosponsors predicted for a bill endorsed by one of the groups with the greatest social power
securing an endorsement from a single socially powerful organization is the best strategy to build support for his or her legislation
As expected, Interest Group Count is positive and statistically significant in predicting whether a bill passes the House
Members have fewer bills competing for their attention, they are receiving input from more sources as multiple interest groups engage in direct lobbying, and the stakes are higher
In the earliest stages of the legislative process, bills that are vetted by an outside organization of high social power send a strong signal that they are worth considering
do not appear to have a direct effect at the end of the legislative process
Indeed, it takes a relatively large list of groups to have a substantively meaningful effect on the probability of passage.
Legislators in search of cosponsors would be wise to find a particularly well-connected group to note in their Dear Colleague letters.

summary_md: Box-Steffensmeier, Christenson and Craig (AJPS 63(1), 2019; online 2018) study 6,633 House bills that were the subject of supportive Dear Colleague letters, 106th to 111th Congresses (1999-2010; regression N = 6,597). They code the interest groups named as endorsers in each letter and measure two signals: Interest Group Social Power, the highest standardized eigenvector centrality of any endorser in the amicus curiae co-signing network, and Interest Group Count, the number of endorsers. In a negative binomial model of cosponsor counts with Congress fixed effects, both are positive (0.055 and 0.007, p<.001). Predicted cosponsors rise from 33 with no endorsement to 51 with a top-centrality endorser; 61 average-centrality endorsers are needed to match that. Logit models of committee reporting and House passage show no direct social-power effect. Count predicts passage (0.013) but not reporting. Cosponsor count predicts both later stages (0.002, 0.004). Majority-party sponsorship (1.353) and hot-bill status (2.428) are the largest passage predictors. The paper has no causal design. Endorsements may be solicited by the sponsor's office, and estimates are pooled across six Congresses and both parties. For Paul's systems, the paper is mainly a source of features and a set of caveats. No built component uses endorsement or group-signal data. The cosponsor forecaster has only member-dyad features, so bill-level outside-support signals are a possible addition. Any LDA-based substitute must respect D-021, however. The legislative pillar's efficiency term credits raw advancement rates without the majority-party adjustment that this paper's passage model shows matters. The solicitation ambiguity matches the system's finding that the lobbied-member link is circular.

Predicted cosponsors: 33 for a bill endorsed only by unconnected groups (score -0.2053) or with no endorsements; 38 with centrality 2.51 (Anti-Defamation League); 51 with centrality 7.66 (Planned Parenthood).

extraction.title: Psychological Aspects of Natural Language Use: Our Words, Our Selves
extraction.venue: Annual Review of Psychology, 54:547-77 (first published online as a Review in Advance, August 14, 2002)
extraction.document_type: Narrative review article (Annual Review chapter); no primary data collected
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1,681 numbered lines of the extracted text, covering article pp. 547-572 and the reference list pp. 573-577. The text file on disk is 99,003 bytes, not the 97,932 characters stated in the task hint; the metadata hint was correct. Paul's markup: none exists for this item (the task listed no markup files), so paul_markup is empty and no highlights, underlines or notes were reviewed. Studies summarized in the review were not read separately; their numbers are as reported by the authors.
extraction.research_question: Can natural word use (open-ended speech and writing, read as style rather than content) serve as a reliable individual-difference marker and as a window onto social, situational, psychological and health processes; and which methods of counting words are available and useful (stated at p. 548)?
extraction.theory: Word use is treated as a psychological marker, with the strongest emphasis on function words ("particles": pronouns, articles, prepositions, conjunctions, auxiliary verbs). The authors argue particles encode shared reference, social identity and self-focus, and cognitive style. Background traditions cited include psychoanalysis (Freud 1901; Lacan 1968), Ricoeur's account of how descriptions define meaning, Goffman's dramaturgy, politeness theory (Brown & Levinson 1987), communication accommodation theory, and verbal immediacy (Wiener & Mehrabian 1968). The review says no compelling psychological theory of word usage yet exists (p. 572). Narrative-writing and disclosure theory (Pennebaker & Francis 1996) is used to explain health effects through coherent narrative construction and shifts in perspective.
extraction.data: None collected by the authors. The review summarizes evidence from many sources: General Inquirer and LIWC studies; Biber's corpus of 481 texts (about 1,000,000 words) across 23 genres (p. 554); Pennebaker & King (1999) writing samples from diaries, college essays and journal abstracts (p. 555); Mehl & Pennebaker (2002a) electronically activated recorder (EAR) samples of everyday conversation from 52 college students (p. 557); a cross-sectional age analysis of more than 3,000 participants from 45 studies, 21 labs and 3 countries, plus 10 authors (p. 556); Mulac et al. (2001) review of more than 30 gender studies (p. 557); Pennebaker & King (1999) Big Five correlations; Newman et al. (2002) five laboratory deception studies (p. 564); Giuliani's 14 press conferences during his first 5 years in office (p. 565); about 15 students wearing EARs after September 11, 2001 (p. 566); Princess Diana online chat groups (p. 566). Sample sizes for most cited health and clinical studies are not reported in the review. Periods covered span roughly 1941 to 2002, with many citations marked "submitted", "in press" or unpublished.
extraction.method: Narrative review organized in sections: (1) six word-count and pattern-analysis methods (General Inquirer, TAS/C, Weintraub's verbal analysis, DICTION, LIWC, Biber factor analysis; LSA as a pattern approach), pp. 549-555; (2) psychometric reliability of word use, pp. 555-556; (3) demographic, personality, mood, need-state, self-esteem and psychopathology links, pp. 556-562; (4) situational, social, deception, upheaval and marital links, pp. 562-567; (5) word use and psychological and health change, including LIWC-based writing-intervention analyses and LSA pronoun-shift analyses, pp. 567-570; (6) discussion of which word classes to study and limitations, pp. 570-572. The review does not pool effects statistically and reports most effects as correlations, percentages or qualitative patterns.
extraction.identification: Not applicable. The review contains no causal identification strategy of its own. Causal language is used loosely in places (e.g., pronoun use "predicting" health changes, p. 569), and the authors note bidirectional effects, particularly in social accommodation (p. 558).
extraction.scope: Psychology, primarily English-language and largely US-based work, with some European and cross-cultural studies cited. Participants are mostly college students, clinical or patient samples, disclosure-study volunteers, public figures (Giuliani, Watergate transcripts, US presidents), novelists and poets, and online chat or everyday-conversation samples. The authors explicitly say they do not cover non-English languages, spoken versus written differences in depth, second-language learners or intelligence (p. 573). Political and campaign speech is discussed only briefly (Hart's DICTION, presidential speeches, Winter 1973, Zullow et al. 1988; pp. 552-553). Nothing on lobbying, legislators, elections, networks or allocation is presented as a finding.

key_findings.finding: Word-use measures show temporal stability. Across 21 language categories in 5-minute talks, successive 2-minute intervals correlated on average at 0.51 (Gleser et al. 1959). Students' everyday conversation was re-sampled four weeks apart with test-retest r of 0.41 for standard linguistic variables and 0.24 for psychological-process variables.
key_findings.location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.51 (21 categories, 2-min intervals); r = 0.41 standard variables, r = 0.24 psychological processes (EAR, Mehl & Pennebaker 2002a)

key_findings.finding: Word use is consistent across topic and social context, so it can be treated as an individual-difference measure. Pennebaker & King (1999) found good internal consistency across text types for 36 LIWC dimensions, and word use was stable across home versus public and work versus amusement settings.
key_findings.location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use, pp. 555-556
key_findings.numbers: 36 LIWC dimensions; text samples from diaries, essays and abstracts written across days and years

key_findings.finding: Language changes with age. Older participants used more positive and fewer negative emotion words, fewer first-person singular references, more future tense and fewer past-tense verbs, and more cognitive-complexity words. Both the cross-sectional study and the novelist/poet longitudinal study converged.
key_findings.numbers: More than 3,000 participants, 45 studies, 21 labs, 3 countries; 60 text dimensions; 10 authors

key_findings.finding: Gender differences in word use are reported across studies, but the evidence is uneven. Mulac et al. (2001) found relatively unambiguous effects for 16 features; men used more quantity references, judgmental adjectives, directives and I-references, while women used more intensifiers, emotion references, uncertainty verbs, negations and hedges. Tag questions showed no consistent difference. In everyday conversations of 52 students, men used nearly four times as many swear words, and women used more filler words and positive-emotion references.
key_findings.numbers: More than 30 studies, 16 features; 52 college students (EAR); men about 4x swear words

key_findings.finding: Big Five self-reports correlate only modestly with word use. Pennebaker & King (1999) reported correlations of 0.10 to 0.16. Neuroticism related to more negative and fewer positive emotion words and more first-person singular; extraversion to positive emotion and social-process words; agreeableness to more positive and fewer negative emotion words.
key_findings.location: Traditional Personality Measures, The Big Five, p. 559
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.10 to 0.16 (Pennebaker & King 1999, multiple writing samples from several hundred college students)

key_findings.finding: Judges' ratings of text emotionality correlated more strongly with language than writers' or speakers' self-reported emotionality did, which raises the question of which personality 'gold standard' to rely on.
key_findings.numbers: Two studies cited (Pennebaker & Francis 1996; Berry et al. 1997); no coefficients given in the review

key_findings.finding: Depression and mania are linked to elevated first-person singular use. Currently depressed students used more I (not me/my/mine) in personal essays. Suicidal poets used fewer first-person plural and more first-person singular pronouns and more death words than nonsuicidal poets. Manic patients used first-person singular more often. The review reads this as self-preoccupation.
key_findings.location: Mental Health and Psychopathology, Depression and Suicidality, pp. 560-561
key_findings.numbers: 18 suicidal and nonsuicidal poets (Stirman & Pennebaker 2001); 10 manic patients (Lorenz & Cobb 1952); sample for Rude et al. (2002) not given in review

key_findings.finding: Physical health links are sparse but suggestive. First-person singular use in structured Type A interviews (self-involvement) related to coronary outcomes and remained significant after controlling for age, cholesterol, smoking and Type A behavior. Positive emotion words in autobiographical sketches from nuns predicted longer life expectancy.
key_findings.location: Physical Health and Health Behavior, pp. 561-562
key_findings.numbers: Scherwitz and colleagues (no effect sizes given); 80 nuns (Danner et al. 2001; no effect sizes given)

key_findings.finding: Deception shows word-level signatures. Across five laboratory studies, truth-tellers used more first-person singular pronouns and more exclusive words (but, except, without) than liars, and liars showed slight but consistent elevations in negative emotion words.
key_findings.numbers: Five laboratory studies (Newman et al. 2002); effect sizes not reported in review

key_findings.finding: Shared and personal upheavals shift pronoun use. After Princess Diana's death, first-person plural in chat groups rose 135% and I fell 12% for about a week, returning to normal by 10 days. In the weeks after September 11, students' first-person plural rose and first-person singular fell for at least 5 days. Texas A&M bonfire coverage doubled first-person plural and negative emotion words and cut big words by more than 10%. During personal crises, Giuliani's first-person singular almost tripled in the period after his diagnosis and related events.
key_findings.location: Emotional Upheavals, Personal and Shared Upheavals, pp. 565-566
key_findings.numbers: +135% first-person plural, -12% I (Diana chat groups); about 15 students (EAR, 9/11); doubling of first-person plural (Texas A&M); 14 press conferences (Giuliani, first 5 years)

key_findings.finding: Social interaction and marriage show word-level coordination and relational markers. Highly involved strangers used more certainty expressions, verbal immediacy and relational pronouns. Chat-room dyads matched each other's function-word and affect-word use turn by turn. Satisfied, traditional married couples used more we and less I.
key_findings.numbers: 120 participants (Cegala 1989); Sillars et al. (1997) large married-couple sample, numbers not given in review

key_findings.finding: Expressive writing about emotional upheavals improves health, and the best predictor is a rise in cognitive words over the writing days. Positive emotion words were linearly related to health gains, while negative emotion words showed an inverted-U relation. Changes in cognitive words explained more variance in health improvement than emotion words. Three independent labs reported related effects, including lymphocyte counts and working memory up to 12 weeks.
key_findings.location: Word Use as a Reflection of Psychological and Health Change, pp. 567-569
key_findings.numbers: Writing typically 3-5 days, 15-30 min/day; six writing studies (Pennebaker et al. 1997); Petrie et al. (1999) medical students; Klein & Boals (2001) working memory

key_findings.finding: Pronoun style, not content, tracks health. Day-to-day pronoun shifts among trauma writers correlated 0.3 to 0.5 with changes in physician visits across three studies. LSA content similarity between days showed no relation to health in three writing studies.
key_findings.location: References to Self and Others, pp. 569-570
key_findings.numbers: r = 0.3 to 0.5 (three studies, Campbell & Pennebaker 2002); LSA: no relation (three studies)

key_findings.finding: Particles dominate word use and are the most psychologically informative. Fewer than 200 common particles account for over half of the words people use, and emotion words are under 5% of words in speech and writing, so emotion-word counts predict emotional state weakly.
key_findings.location: Which Words Should We Be Studying?, pp. 570-571
key_findings.numbers: Under 200 particles = over 50% of words; emotion words under 5% of words

key_findings.finding: Word-count methods differ in scope: Biber's factor analysis of 481 texts (about 1,000,000 words) from 23 genres yielded 6 factors; LIWC searches over 2,300 words in more than 70 dimensions; DICTION uses 10,000 search words with 5 master variables and 35 subfeatures, normed on 20,000 samples; TAS/C uses about 2,000 emotion words and 3,900 abstraction entries. Word-count methods are reliable and efficient but ignore context, irony and sarcasm.
key_findings.numbers: Biber 481 texts / ~1,000,000 words / 23 genres / 67 variables / 6 factors; LIWC 2,300+ words / 70+ dimensions; DICTION 10,000 words / 5 master variables / 35 subfeatures / 20,000 norm samples; TAS/C 2,000+ / 3,900

limitations: Word counts cannot capture context, irony, sarcasm or multiple word meanings, and many communication constructs (ingroup-outgroup status, formality, requests) are not easily detected (pp. 572-573).
No compelling psychological theory of word usage yet exists (p. 572); Zeldow & McAdams (1993) questioned whether lower-level word counts have psychological meaning.
Gender findings rest on a few studies with small samples and one text source; several key claims come from exclusively nonpersonal writings (pp. 557-558).
Gender effects may reflect social engagement or power rather than sex, and language use may show bidirectional effects, e.g., accommodation to partners (pp. 558, 555-558).
Personality self-report correlations are small (r about 0.10-0.16) and are not clearly superior to judge ratings (pp. 559-560).
Clinical studies are often small, use inconsistent inclusion criteria, and lack proper control groups (pp. 560-561).
Health-linked evidence is sparse, often unpublished or submitted, and effect sizes are not reported for several key studies (pp. 561-562).
Unclear whether a sample predicting one outcome (e.g., positive words in an essay) generalizes to psychological or physical phenomena more broadly (p. 562).
Content-based dictionaries have performed poorly because topics are almost infinite and categories are culture-bound (p. 571).
Review omits cross-language comparison, written versus spoken differences in depth, second-language learning, intelligence and stereotype communication (p. 573).
Several cited studies are 'submitted', 'in press' or unpublished, so their results could not be checked against final publications from this text alone.

summary_md:
Pennebaker, Mehl and Niederhoffer (2003) is a narrative review with no new data. It argues that the way people use words, especially function words such as pronouns, articles and negations, works as a stable individual-difference marker. Their reliability evidence is moderate. Successive 2-minute speech segments correlate at r = 0.51 across 21 categories. Four-week test-retest correlations of everyday speech are 0.41 for standard linguistic categories and only 0.24 for psychological-process categories. The link to personality is weak. Big Five self-reports correlate with word use at r = 0.10 to 0.16 in a few hundred students. Neuroticism goes with more negative-emotion words, fewer positive-emotion words and more first-person singular. Depression is tied to "I" specifically, not me, my or mine. Emotion words make up under 5% of all words, so emotion counts are a weak readout of emotional state. Raters who judge a text's emotionality agree with its language more closely than the writers' own self-reports do. The authors also note that word counts ignore context and irony.

For Paul's systems, this is the stated source for the Pennebaker LIWC base in the affective-N slot, and through Pennebaker and King (1999) for the fallback trait weights in the lexical Big Five. As built, both of those direct uses are now dormant or have moved. Since round 7b, the LIWC base in affective N is only a convergent-validity anchor (r = +.24) and is no longer part of the score. The Pennebaker–King weights in big5_traits.py are overridden whenever mairesse_smoreg.json is present, and it is present. The review's main value here is calibration. With word-trait correlations of r = 0.10 to 0.16, a mean held-out r of .350 against RKH is more than this literature supports, which is consistent with the method-shared inflation the system already records. The low reliability of psychological-process categories also makes the system's failed cross-genre transfers unsurprising. The evidence comes from US college students writing spontaneously. It does not cover staff-written press or floor ritual.

summary_issues: The successive 2-minute r = 0.51 is from Gleser et al. 1959 on 5-minute talks, not the review own data. The summary should attribute it.
The 0.41 and 0.24 retest figures are Mehl and Pennebaker 2002a EAR data from 52 college students. The summary should attribute them.
Judge sentence: the summary says judges agree with its language more closely. The paper says ratings correlated more highly with language than with self-reports, in at least two studies.

Evidence source: the summary says US college students. The review mixes student self-reports, diaries, journal abstracts, poets, elderly depressed speakers and chat-room dyads, and states no country for these samples.
Depression: the I-only effect comes from student personal essays (Rude et al. 2002), not a clinical sample. The summary omits the sample.

The mean held-out r of .350 against RKH, and the claim the literature cannot support it, are analyst comparisons across different measures, not paper findings. The .350 figure was not located in the fec/members code or docs searched.
The claim that low reliability of psychological-process categories makes failed cross-genre transfers unsurprising is an inference. The review does not discuss genre transfer.
Function-word gap: the review names particles as a research priority and I-to-we as a shared-upheaval signal. It does not call them the most informative signal.
Shared-upheaval figures (135 percent, 12 percent, back to normal by day 10) come from one online chat-room study after Princess Diana death (Stone and Pennebaker 2002), not a general pattern.
Ghost-writing and authorship are not discussed in the review. That gap is the analyst's, not paper content.
Page errors: the Big Five passage is p. 558, not 559; the judges passage is p. 559 under Traditional Personality Measures, not Summary p. 560.

gaps_exposed: Function-word style is a gap. The paper treats pronoun and particle shifts (I to we, exclusive words, articles) as the most informative signal, but the stance and press layers use only content dictionaries (LSD) and NLI. No style-based signal exists, and none has been validated. This is listed as a gap only and is not a recommendation.

Transient event windows are not handled. Shared upheavals raised first-person plural by 135% and cut 'I' by 12% for about a week, returning to baseline by day 10. The trait readers pool text across time with no exclusion window around shocks, so crisis-period speech could move member-level N or E scores.

There is no linguistic-synchrony measure. The paper shows turn-by-turn function-word matching in dyads (Niederhoffer & Pennebaker 2002). The co-appearance layer records only that two members appeared together, not whether their speech converged. Any such measure would be UNVERIFIED new analysis until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

Ghost-writing and genre authorship are not modelled. The paper's individual-difference claims rest on self-authored spontaneous text, and the system has no per-genre authorship weight beyond C_INT_W and RITUAL stripping.

The note is stale on both points and the component description repeats the error.

The component assumption 'Negative-emotion and first-person-singular words track N (Pennebaker)' overstates the source. The paper reports r = 0.10 to 0.16 against student self-reports, and its depression evidence is specific to 'I', while the system's FPS regex pools me/my/mine/myself.

paul_alignment: Paul left no annotations on this paper. His positions on affective-n ('No annotation addresses it directly', citing Ramey) and lexical-big5 (Ramey 'dated but foundational'; Birkenmaier's criticism of unvalidated SVM) are consistent with what this review shows. The review supplies the modest effect-size ceiling (r = 0.10 to 0.16) that Paul's notes lack, and it supports his preference for venue-specific frameworks, since its reliability evidence comes from self-authored student text. Paul is not stale here, but the brain's description of the affective-N measure is stale (see flags).

extraction.research_question: Estimate the mean predictive validity (Pearson r) of social-media digital footprints for each Big 5 trait; test whether the types of footprint used, the platform's default privacy setting (public vs. private), and study quality moderate prediction accuracy; check for publication bias; and assess whether accuracy is consistent across traits (Abstract; Sec. 1.3, p.151).
extraction.theory: Social-media content is an extension of "one's self" and reflects actual personality rather than idealized self-presentation (Back et al., 2010; Seidman, 2013), so digital footprints should carry personality signal (Sec. 1.1, p.150). Benchmark: the typical behavior-personality correlation of about 0.30-0.40, the "personality coefficient" (Meyer et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2007), which the authors call the "correlational upper-limit" (Abstract; Sec. 4, p.155). The Big 5 (McCrae & Costa, 1987; McCrae & John, 1992) is the target framework (Sec. 1.2, p.151). No formal theory of why particular footprints predict particular traits is developed; the moderator hypotheses come from survey literature on demographics and from the extraversion-activity link.
extraction.data: Unit: independent study-level effect size. Literature (Scopus, ISI Web of Science, PubMed, ProQuest, plus Google/Google Scholar and citation chasing), search finalized May 2017 (Sec. 2.1, p.151-152). 24 papers and 28 studies identified (Sec. 3.1, p.154). Removed 12 studies for non-independence: 11 used MyPersonality (Facebook) data, plus Golbeck (2016) Study 3 (shared data with Golbeck et al., 2011). Final set: 14 papers, 16 independent studies, 80 effect sizes (16 per trait). Platforms in the 16: Facebook 7, Twitter 5, Sina Weibo 3, Instagram+Twitter 1. Footprints: 9 single-type studies, 7 multiple-type. Five papers lacked usable effect sizes; author contact recovered one; four were excluded (Sec. 2.4, p.153). Participant N and study years are not reported in the extracted text; the pooled N is not stated. Coders: the authors, with full agreement reported (Sec. 2.4, p.154).
extraction.method:
Five separate random-effects meta-analyses, one per Big 5 trait, using untransformed Pearson r (Fisher z explicitly rejected, citing Schmidt & Hunter, 2014; Sec. 2.4, p.153). Conversions: R^2 to r by square root (n=2); AUROC to Cohen's d to r (n=1); sensitivity/specificity or PPV/NPV to odds ratio to d to r (n=1); non-r reports converted (n=4). Where a study had several models or features, the best model or highest feature effect was used (Sec. 2.4, p.152-153). Outliers: Grubbs test (none found). Heterogeneity: Q, tau^2, I^2. Publication bias: funnel plot, Begg-Mazumdar and Egger tests, trim-and-fill, classic fail-safe N. Moderators: univariate random-effects meta-regression, REML, alpha 0.05, p<0.10 discussed; a moderator was tested only if at least 4 studies per group (Fu et al., 2014). Quality groups were pooled as low+medium (2+2) vs high (12) to reach the minimum. Software: Comprehensive Meta-analysis v3.3.070 (Sec. 2.4, p.153-154; Sec. 3.2.3, p.154).</method>

summary_md:
Azucar, Marengo and Settanni (Personality and Individual Differences 124, 2018; online December 2017) pooled 16 independent studies from 14 papers. They ran one random-effects meta-analysis per trait on untransformed Pearson r. The criterion in every study was a self-report Big Five inventory (BFI, TIPI or IPIP) from ordinary users of Facebook, Twitter, Sina Weibo or Instagram, with literature searched up to May 2017. The pooled correlations were: Openness .39, Conscientiousness .35, Extraversion .40, Agreeableness .29 (the lowest) and Neuroticism .33. The authors found no publication bias. Heterogeneity was very large (I² ≥ 93.15, every Q(15) significant). In univariate meta-regressions, using several types of footprint raised accuracy for O, C and N. Adding demographics raised it for A and N. Activity statistics (friends, posts, network density) raised it for E only marginally (β .19, p .06). Text and pictures alone added nothing. The pooled numbers are optimistic, because each study contributed its best model or strongest feature.

For Paul's systems this is a calibration paper, not a validation of them. Melange scores members of Congress, whose posts and press output are written by staff, against RKH estimates, which are themselves derived from text, and against Senate expert and insider panels. Neither of those is self-report from the members. The lexical reader's held-out CV against RKH has a mean of .350. That sits inside Azucar's range by coincidence of scale, not by comparable design, so it should never be presented as matching the meta-analytic benchmark. The paper offers three sharper lessons:
- Agreeableness is the least recoverable trait from digital footprints, which supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioural cooperation.
- Activity counts are at best a marginal Extraversion signal.
- Demographics improve "accuracy" only because group membership correlates with self-reported traits. The system's affective-N gate removes exactly that signal on purpose.

These pooled figures cover 16 studies of lay users and are UNSTRATIFIED across platforms. The authors could not test differences between platforms.

summary_issues: Held-out CV figures are not in the repo: the summary's 'held-out CV against RKH mean .350' and the claim that it sits inside Azucar's range by coincidence should be removed. Repo held-out r in data/members/big5_v2.json are against behavioral targets: A .059, C .281, E .563, O .135; ES has none.

The summary says the pooled numbers are optimistic. The paper does not say that. It says each study contributed its best model or strongest feature, which may inflate the pooled r; rewrite as a possibility.

The summary says demographics improve accuracy only because group membership correlates with self-reported traits. The paper does not establish that mechanism; it cites survey literature on demographic differences in self-report. Rewrite as a hypothesis.
The summary says the affective-N gate removes exactly the demographic signal. The residualization in emit_affective_n.py controls for party and E only; age and gender are not controlled.
The summary says Agreeableness supports the system's move from lexical A to behavioral cooperation. The paper tests no system; at most it is consistent with the move. Reword accordingly.

The summary says Melange's Congress data is staff-written and that the system is validated against Senate expert and insider panels. Neither is in the paper, and neither was checked in the code read here. Mark as unverified.
Bearing 1 says O is the best-predicted trait in Azucar. This is false: E (.40) is highest and O (.39) second. Corrected in the bearing.

The paper's Table 1 asterisks do not match its exclusion text: Farnadi 2016 Study 3 is asterisked but its Twitter data is needed for the 7/5/3/1 platform split, and Golbeck 2016 Study 3 is excluded in the text but not asterisked. The platform split reconciles with the text's inclusion list, so the asterisks should not be used.

The paper's own text says 11 MyPersonality studies plus Golbeck 2016 Study 3 were excluded, and that two MyPersonality-based studies (Farnadi 2016 Study 1; Kosinski 2013) were included. The summary's 'ordinary users' description should note the two included MyPersonality studies.

Paul alignment section: the item has no Paul annotations (paul_entries is empty and the ext coverage notes none found), so attributions to Paul's views and to his receptivity-layer notes cannot be verified. Remove or mark unverified.

Ext note: the Bachrach 2012 ad-targeting claim sits on p.157 (Conclusions), not p.156. The Kosinski 2014 conscientiousness finding is fewer pictures, fewer Likes and less group activity, not a general 'post less'.

Bearing 5 and the flags: the summary's suggestion that the hybrid gives directional support for footprint combination conflicts with the artifact's held-out numbers, which show no gain over lexical-only on any target.
gaps_exposed: No self-report criterion exists for legislators. The system's references (RKH text estimates, Senate expert and insider panels) are not the criterion the footprint literature validates against, so the paper's accuracy figures cannot be imported as a benchmark.

Authorship: the system does not model staff or ghost-writing in social posts and press output, although the meta-analysis's theoretical warrant (content as an extension of the self) assumes the person wrote it.

Per-platform and per-genre accuracy: the paper could not stratify by platform, and the system pools tweets, floor speech and interviews into one corpus (BIG5_SOURCES restricts genres for validation only). No stratified accuracy by genre is reported against an external criterion.

Upward bias from model selection: the paper's best-model-per-study rule inflates pooled r. The system's own improvement rounds guard against this with single looks, but no comparison to a lay-user benchmark accounts for it.
flags: Do not quote 'remarkable accuracy' or pooled r ≈ .35 as evidence that Melange's lexical Big Five (CV vs RKH mean .350) is valid. The criteria differ, RKH shares the reader's method, and the pooled figure spans I² ≥ 93% heterogeneity. Any citation must carry the label UNSTRATIFIED (16 studies, 4 platforms, lay users, 2012-2017).

The demographics-moderator finding must not be used to justify adding party or gender as trait predictors. That conflicts with the affective-N gate (party-controlled, party r = .000) and would make a group proxy look like a personality measure.

The big5_traits.py docstring treats social posts as validated personality-cue carriers (citing Birkenmaier). Azucar's evidence concerns self-authored lay-user content, so it does not extend that claim to staff-managed congressional accounts.
No conflict with the rejected SNA proposals, D-021 or D-025: the paper makes no network-edge or influence claims.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It agrees with his call for frameworks specific to each venue: the paper's platform heterogeneity is large and it could not test differences across platforms. It also fits his view that A collapses into a smaller set of observable dispositions. It does not support his more optimistic plan to use psychological traits as edge parameters in the receptivity layer. Even among lay users with authentic self-report, A is the least recoverable trait (r = .29), and the paper says nothing about whether traits predict yielding to pressure. His notes about the receptivity layer and lexical Big Five predate the nomological indictment and the behavioural basis now running in receptivity_layer.py. The paper agrees with the system as currently built more than with those older notes.

extraction.research_question: Do redistricting commissions used in the 2010 round produce congressional district maps that are biased toward one party compared with a neutral, partisan-blind standard drawn within the same state? The paper asks how well commissions perform as neutral decision makers, using the 2010 round as the test.
extraction.theory: Gerrymandering harms two things: (1) exclusion or silencing of minority-party voters via vote cracking (exclusionary gerrymander, indicated by a smaller-than-expected standard deviation in district vote shares with minimal minority opportunity to win), and (2) entrenchment of a majority party regardless of its vote share via packing (indicated by skew in the district vote distribution, median minus mean). Total electoral bias = turnout bias + gerrymandering bias (asymmetry due to skew). Commissions are expected to act like a divided government, with bipartisan members producing bias toward whichever side gains an upper hand, or to produce neutral lines if bipartisanship works (pp. 381-383, 384, 390).
extraction.data: Unit: state congressional district plans (enacted maps) and statewide two-party vote returns by voter tabulation district (VTD). Sample: 34 states that could be evaluated, of which 7 use commissions (independent: AZ, CA, WA; advisory: IA, NY, VA; politician: NJ). Excluded 16 states: 12 with one or two districts, KY and OR (no VTD data), OK and WV (insufficient partisan predictability). Period: 2010 redistricting round; elections analyzed 2008-2014 in Table 4 and Table A (e.g., AZ 2008-2012 statewide, NJ 2008-2013, VA 2008-2013); the text also cites 2016-2020 House results for AZ and VA. Simulated baseline: 10,000 computer-generated plans per state. Vote data: Daily Kos (Wolf) estimates disaggregating county returns to VTDs using 2008 presidential shares; Census VTD shapefiles. Validation of vote estimates against official VTD tallies in WI, NC, FL: correlations 0.87-0.97 (p. 383). N for the sample: 34 states, 7 commission states, 10,000 maps per state (~340,000 simulated plans).
extraction.method: Descriptive counterfactual-comparison design with a simulated neutral baseline. Each enacted map is compared with the distribution of outcomes from 10,000 partisan-blind plans per state, generated with the Magleby and Mosesson (2018) multi-level weighted graph-partitioning algorithm (rook contiguity, population balance within about plus or minus 1%, compactness considered in the appendix). Indicators: observed vs expected standard deviation of Democratic district vote share (exclusion); observed vs expected gerrymandering bias (median minus mean district vote share, skew/entrenchment); turnout bias (mean district vote share minus statewide vote share); observed vs expected number of districts won by the statewide Democratic candidate (majority-rule test). Evaluation is on average values across states and elections (Figures 2-3), then state-by-state (Table 4, Figure 4 traces of observed vs expected district vote shares, sorted low to high). For Arizona, the two Hispanic majority-minority districts were held fixed in all simulated plans (Appendix, VRA section). Compactness compared via dispersion (area / minimum circumscribing circle) and perimeter (Niemi et al. 1990) ratios for 1,000 simulated maps vs the commission map.
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. The comparison to a neutral within-state simulated baseline is the counterfactual for how a partisan-blind process would sort voters across districts given residential geography. Cross-state comparisons are explicitly rejected because geography differs across states (p. 380). The paper does not estimate treatment effects of commissions versus legislatures using a causal design; its cross-state commission-vs-legislature comparison (Figures 2-3) is descriptive.
extraction.scope: Population: 34 states with at least three congressional districts and usable VTD data, US House districts, 2010 redistricting round. Institutions: 7 states with redistricting commissions (3 independent, 3 advisory, 1 politician commission; the paper labels NJ politician and Hawaii politician; see Table 1), plus legislative and court-imposed plans in other states. Era: post-2010 maps used in 2012-2014 House elections (with later 2016-2020 references for AZ and VA). Scope is congressional, not state legislative, districts.

key_findings.finding: Three of seven commission states produced suspect results benefiting one party: Arizona pro-Democratic; New Jersey and Virginia pro-Republican. Commissions generally produce less partisan bias than legislatures, but do not always eliminate it.
key_findings.location: Abstract p. 379; Introduction pp. 380-381; Evaluations p. 385-386
key_findings.numbers: 3 of 7 commission states flagged; 34 states evaluated; 10,000 simulated maps per state

key_findings.finding: Across the 34 evaluated states, maps enacted by commission states generally perform better (closer to neutral baseline) than maps enacted by states without commissions.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative; commission states mostly near or below the 45-degree lines; AZ, NJ, VA above the line in Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Arizona (independent commission): turnout bias favored Democrats about 2 points across all 10 statewide 2008-2012 elections. Enacted plan added roughly 1.5 points of pro-Democratic asymmetry bias beyond what residential patterns would produce, erasing a neutral pro-Republican asymmetry. Republicans charged mistreatment and the commission's map was judged a pro-Democratic gerrymander.
key_findings.location: Suspect 1, pp. 387-388; Table 4 p. 387; Conclusion p. 390
key_findings.numbers: turnout bias about +2 points; added asymmetry about +1.5 points; expected asymmetry balanced by pro-Republican bias under neutral drawing

key_findings.finding: Arizona: enacted standard deviations were consistently larger than expected (more dispersed, less competitive districts), with packing in both directions; Democrats carried the three CDs they were described as making more competitive. The contramajoritarian result was limited: Republicans won 5 of 9 seats in 2014 and 2016, so Democrats were not entrenched.
key_findings.numbers: Obama 2012 at 45.4% of two-party vote carried 5 of 9 seats; Democratic Senate candidate 48.4% in 2012 would have carried 5 of 9 seats with CDs 1, 2, 9 over 50%; Republicans won 5 of 9 House seats in 2014 and 2016

key_findings.finding: New Jersey (political commission, party-line 7-6 vote favored the Republican plan): enacted lines show an anti-Democratic gerrymander bias of 1.7 to 3.7 points, partly offset by 1.3 to 2.5 points of pro-Democratic turnout bias. Standard deviations uniformly larger than the neutral average.
key_findings.location: Suspect 2, p. 389; Table 4 p. 387; Conclusion p. 391
key_findings.numbers: gerrymander bias against Democrats 1.7-3.7 points; turnout bias +1.3 to +2.5; 2013 Senate special: Democrat 55.5% carried 6 of 12 districts

key_findings.finding: Virginia (advisory commission, plan actually chosen by the legislature after an inconclusive session and a 20-20 Senate tie broken by the Republican Lieutenant Governor): a pro-Republican gerrymander, persistently biased against Democrats in all 10 observed elections; asymmetry of 2.7-4.0 points; fewer than 1% of partisan-blind plans exceed the observed asymmetry, except Warner's abnormally lopsided 2008 Senate win.
key_findings.location: Suspect 3, pp. 389-390; Table 4 p. 387; Conclusion p. 390
key_findings.numbers: asymmetry bias 2.7-4.0 points against Democrats in 10 of 10 elections; Obama 2012 won 52% of two-party vote and carried 4 of 11 districts; Democrats won 3 of 11 House races in 2012 and 2014; 4 of 5 elections with Democratic vote share 50-54% failed to carry a majority of districts

key_findings.finding: California (independent) slightly reduced but did not eliminate anti-Democratic bias from residential patterns; Washington (independent) drew a plan that allowed residential-pattern consequences to stand; no evidence of gerrymandering in either. Iowa and New York maps fall in line with the neutral standard; Iowa may be somewhat more competitive than residential patterns alone.
key_findings.location: Suspect discussion pp. 386-387 and Conclusion pp. 390; Table A p. 392
key_findings.numbers: CA 53 districts; IA 4 districts (55% vote share won all four seats by both parties per text); NY 27 districts (2010 Comptroller: Democrat 52% carried 11 of 27)

key_findings.finding: Commissions do well on charges (population equality, contiguity, compactness, jurisdictional boundaries, competitiveness) and produce maps closer to the partisan-blind standard than legislatures, but the same cannot be said uniformly for avoiding partisan gerrymanders. The authors argue commissions are decidedly bipartisan, and that the charges given to them focus on form rather than a substantive anti-gerrymander standard.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative

key_findings.finding: Arizona's enacted map is compact on the dispersion measure relative to algorithm-drawn maps: its median district's dispersion ratio (0.4797) exceeds the median district in 95.8% of 1,000 simulated maps; simulated maps show lower variance in compactness than the commission map (86.95% lower on dispersion SD; 99.8% lower on perimeter SD).

limitations: Vote-share data are estimates: Daily Kos disaggregation of county returns to VTDs using 2008 presidential shares. Validation correlations of 0.87-0.97 were checked only against official VTD tallies in WI, NC, and FL (p. 383).
VTD shapefiles are out of date by the 2012 and 2014 elections because states re-precinct more often than they redistrict; the authors rely on estimated VTD vote totals (fn 10, p. 392).

Results are based on average values across states and elections in the first evaluation; the authors state a closer state-by-state look is required to say whether any suspect state enacted a partisan gerrymander (p. 386-387).
Only 2010-round congressional maps; 16 states excluded (12 with one or two districts, KY and OR lacking VTD data, OK and WV with low partisan predictability) (fn 12).

The neutral baseline imposes only minimalist constraints (contiguity, compactness, equal population, plus fixed Hispanic majority-minority districts in AZ). Simulated maps differ from enacted maps in other ways, and the compactness comparison shows algorithm maps are more uniform, not identical.
The sign/size of the residual bias is a within-state counterfactual; the paper does not claim causal effects of commission design.

Threshold for 'suspect' is an informal statistical standard (observed vs expected values across 10,000 maps; e.g., less than 1% of simulated plans exceeding observed asymmetry); the paper notes standard deviation alone is insufficient to identify partisan gerrymanders because entrenchment requires packing and cracking together (fn 13).
Maryland and Utah are flagged as possible exclusionary (cracking) outliers in fn 13 but are not analyzed in depth.
measures: Statewide two-party Democratic vote share
Mean district vote share (equal-district weighting)
Median district vote share
Turnout bias = mean district vote share minus statewide vote share
Gerrymandering bias (asymmetry/skew) = median district vote share minus mean district vote share
Total electoral bias = turnout bias + gerrymandering bias
Observed vs expected standard deviation of district Democratic vote share (exclusion indicator; expected from 10,000 simulated maps)
Observed vs expected number of districts won by statewide Democratic candidate (majority-rule test)
Compactness: dispersion (district area / minimum circumscribing circle area) and perimeter (district area / area of circle with same perimeter), per Niemi et al. 1990
Observed vs expected gerrymander bias from simulated plans

short_quotes.quote: commissions are decidedly bipartisan, and the maps they create are influenced by politics

bearings.paper_claim: District partisanship is partly a product of how lines are drawn. Compared with 10,000 neutral plans per state, enacted maps added about +1.5 points of pro-Democratic asymmetry (median minus mean) in Arizona, 1.7-3.7 points against Democrats in New Jersey and 2.7-4.0 points against Democrats in Virginia (10 of 10 elections; fewer than 1% of neutral plans as skewed). The Arizona commission's districts had larger SDs than expected, meaning packing in both directions and fewer competitive seats than neutral drawing would produce.
bearings.paper_location: Table 4 p. 387; Suspects 1-3 pp. 387-390; Figure 4 p. 388
bearings.system_side: c = 1 + 1.0*exp(-max(lean,0)/5.0), where lean is the Cook PVI oriented toward the member's party. c scales effective dollars on both money legs. Ten mid-decade redistricted states and PVI shifts of 5 points or more are flagged but never altered. AMPLITUDE and SCALE are uncalibrated owner judgment, and the reciprocity they encode is not validated.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's shifts are state-level skews in two-party vote share. They are not per-district PVI changes, so they show only the order of magnitude by which a map can move lean. Under the model formula, a 3-4 point lean change moves c by roughly 0.45-0.55 near lean 0. That makes c partly a function of map choice, which matters most in the flagged 2025-26 mid-decade redistricted states. The paper covers the 2010 round and congressional districts only, and it says nothing about whether contributions are worth more in competitive seats. It must not be cited as support for the reciprocity premise (D-104..D-108).

bearings.paper_claim: Redistricting materially reshuffles how voters are distributed across districts: the SD and skew of district vote shares differ from neutral by several points. The authors also flag boundary-vintage mismatch (VTD shapefiles out of date because states re-precinct more often than they redistrict) as a limitation on their own estimates.

bearings.system_side: The Census CD scraper stacks ACS metrics on 119th-Congress districts with 2020 CBP establishment counts on 116th-Congress district boundaries. The mismatch is documented and accepted as tolerable.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper is about vote distributions, not business counts. It does not quantify measurement error from mixing boundary vintages. It only reinforces that boundary changes are not innocuous in states that redrew substantially, which includes the 2020-round redraws and the later mid-decade redraws. The paper offers no evidence about how large the CBP error is.

gaps_exposed: The competitiveness multiplier treats Cook PVI lean as given. It has no notion of how much of a seat's safety comes from the map rather than from residential geography. The paper's neutral-ensemble baseline is the standard tool for separating the two, and the system has no equivalent (none is needed unless c is ever calibrated).

Mid-decade redistricted states are flagged in build_competitiveness.py but not treated in any other way. The paper shows that map changes of a few points are routine, which is on the order of SCALE = 5 PVI points, so c in those states depends heavily on which map vintage is used.
flags: The paper does not validate the competitiveness reciprocity (dollars buy more in competitive seats). Reciprocity remains NOT validated (D-104..D-108), and the paper must not be quoted as support for COMPET_MULT.
Era and scope: 2010-round congressional maps, with elections 2008-2014. The live Cook 2026 PVI reflects 2020-round and mid-decade 2025-26 maps that the paper does not cover.

Pooled commission vs legislature comparison (Figures 2-3): any figure taken from it should be labeled UNSTRATIFIED. It averages across states with different geography, which the authors themselves warn against for cross-state comparisons.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotation of this paper. For the competitiveness multiplier, his position is that Cook PVI is a valid vulnerability measure and that competitive seats are responsive. The paper agrees that district partisanship is measurable and consequential, but it adds a caveat his notes do not record: PVI-type lean is partly a product of how the map was drawn, by several points. No source he annotated, including this one, shows that dollars buy more in competitive seats. His note is not stale relative to the system. The system already labels the reciprocity as unvalidated and flags redistricted states.

related.why: Becker shows that formal redistricting criteria can be gamed. Best et al. find that commissions satisfy their formal charges (compactness, contiguity) yet still produced partisan bias in 3 of 7 states, an empirical case of the same weakness.

Same domain: method validation for redistricting analysis. DeLuca validates BISG race estimates for VRA work. Best et al. hold Arizona's majority-minority districts fixed in their neutral ensemble and validate their VTD vote estimates (r = 0.87-0.97).

Cook's district partisanship ratings are the type of measure the competitiveness multiplier consumes. Best et al. show that such district partisanship shifts by 1.5-4 points depending on how the map is drawn.

backlinks.why: Best asks whether commissions avoid partisan gerrymanders. McCartan supplies the outlier-versus-ensemble benchmark such an evaluation needs.

extraction.research_question: Do legislators' social ties with political allies and political adversaries affect how they vote? Specifically, does more social connectedness predict more voting agreement between allies, and less agreement between adversaries (the "keep your friends close and enemies closer" logic)? (pp. 601-603, 609-610)
extraction.theory: Legislators use social contacts as information sources. Ties to allies are valuable when the two agree, and ties to adversaries are valuable when they disagree, because a predictable source of cues helps a legislator confirm or revise a policy position. Legislators therefore form expectations about whether a colleague will agree, and the link between connectedness and voting depends on those expectations (ideology and party are the basis for the expectations). Hypothesis 1: the more socially connected two political adversaries are, the less likely they are to vote the same way. Hypothesis 2: the more socially connected two political allies are, the more likely they are to vote the same way. The authors state the causal direction is simultaneous and endogenous (social ties can drive co-voting, and anticipated co-voting can drive ties) and limit claims to symmetric association (pp. 605-610, 620).
extraction.data: Population of interest: legislative staffers (assistants) of MEPs on the European Parliament's Committee on Environment, Public Health and Food Safety, 2004-2009 term. Network data: web questionnaire (8 responses) and interviews (24, June-July 2007) with staff of 32 of 65 committee members' offices (47% response; 3 members from Bulgaria and Romania were excluded because they joined in January 2007). Full dyadic census of the committee: 65 offices, 4,160 directed or 2,080 symmetric dyads. Dyadic response was 46% for directed reports (1,920 of 4,160) and 71.4% when reports on non-respondents' offices are used. Density was 5.7% on the respondent-alter subnetwork (9.7% if symmetrized) and 6.1% (118 of 1,920 possible ties) on the full asymmetric subnetwork. Voting data: 40 final plenary roll-call votes on Environment Committee bills plus amendments, July 2004 to July 2008 (sixth term). Analysed unit: dyad (pair of MEPs). Observations: 1,920 dyads with network information (1,912 in the OLS and linear models; 1,319 in the log-odds model after dropping 0% and 100% co-voting). Ideology: NOMINATE scores from Hix and Noury (sixth EP). Sample description and missingness tests: Tables 1-2.
extraction.method: Dependent variable is the co-voting rate per dyad (share of roll calls where both voted yes or both no). Model 1: OLS on all observations, presented as misspecified for comparison. Model 2: linear mixed-effects model (lmer, REML) with crossed random effects for respondent and alter, using all observations. Model 3: logit-transformed co-voting rate (log-odds) with random effects for respondent and alter, fitted with lmer and a Laplace approximation, dropping unanimous (0% and 100%) dyads. Predictors: same party, same voting bloc (GUE/NGL plus Greens/EFA vs PES, ALDE, UEN and EPP-ED, inferred from voting; four members belong to neither bloc), same nationality, absolute difference in seniority, point connectivity, and point connectivity x same bloc. Robustness: the authors estimated alternative specifications (lagged votes, joint-membership instrument, reverse-causality models) and report that results are sensitive to specification changes (fn. 81, p. 627); the chosen specification is defended as most theoretically consistent.
extraction.identification: No causal identification strategy. The authors acknowledge a simultaneity or reverse-causality problem (pp. 610, 620, 627). They address (a) non-independence of dyads with crossed random effects for respondent and alter (pp. 623-624), (b) reverse causation partly by controlling for expected co-voting through voting-bloc membership (p. 620), and (c) the ordinal/bounded outcome with a log-odds transform (p. 623). They assume non-respondents are missing at random, and they do not test this beyond comparing response by region (Table 1, chi-square 0.935, p = 0.817) and EU accession date (Table 2, chi-square 0.3752, p = 0.540) (pp. 614-616).
extraction.scope: Population: MEPs on one committee (Environment, Public Health and Food Safety) in the European Parliament, 2004-2009, and their staff networks. Policy area: environment and consumer protection (p. 613). Era: sixth parliamentary term (2004-2008 votes; 2007 survey). The authors frame the theory generally for legislatures (US and EP examples), but the data cover one committee in one policy area with 65 offices, so they caution about generalization (pp. 613, 627-628).

key_findings.finding: Hypothesis 1 supported: higher point connectivity between opposing-bloc MEPs predicts less frequent co-voting, and the coefficient is negative and distinguishable from zero in all three specifications, controlling for party and bloc.
key_findings.numbers: Point connectivity coefficient: OLS -0.0716 (SE 0.0043); linear multilevel -0.0234 (SE 0.0051); log-odds multilevel -0.1020 (SE 0.0307).

key_findings.finding: Log-odds effect size: a one-unit increase in point connectivity lowers the odds of co-voting by about 10 per cent for non-coalition pairs.
key_findings.numbers: Drop of 10% in odds (95% CI 7-13%). On the probability scale, moving from -1 SD (0.6) to +1 SD (3.8) connectivity lowers predicted co-voting for non-coalition pairs from 52% to 44%. A one-unit increase around the median (2) lowers it from 50% to 47%.

key_findings.finding: Baseline: with no social information, opposing-bloc members are predicted to vote together about half the time, which is the empirical mean for such dyads.
key_findings.numbers: Predicted co-voting about 50% at the empirical mean.

key_findings.finding: Same-bloc membership strongly predicts co-voting; joint party membership, nationality and seniority difference do not add explanatory power once bloc is controlled.
key_findings.numbers: Joint bloc membership: OLS 0.3552 (SE 0.0147); linear 0.5590 (SE 0.0135); log-odds 2.9103 (SE 0.0985), i.e., odds roughly 300% higher. Party: 0.0164 / 0.0063 / -0.0953 (none significant). Nationality and seniority: not significant.

key_findings.finding: Hypothesis 2 (allies co-vote more with more connection) cannot be tested with these data because there is almost no variation among same-coalition dyads.
key_findings.numbers: Of 594 same-coalition dyads, 574 (97%) voted together 100% of the time on the forty Environment Committee bills.

key_findings.finding: Co-voting distribution is bimodal: about one-third of all pairs vote together 100% of the time, and the authors therefore drop unanimous observations in the log-odds model.
key_findings.numbers: 1,920 observations; 594 pairs at 100% co-voting; only five pairs at 0%.

key_findings.finding: Connectivity structure: contact is sparse and many pairs are poorly connected, though the measure has a meaningful spread.
key_findings.numbers: Density 5.7% (9.7% symmetric; 6.1% on 118 of 1,920 possible ties). Mean point connectivity 2.2, median 2, maximum 12 (one Spanish EPP and British Conservative pair). 12.4% of dyads have zero connectivity. 39.5% of office pairs are cut off by removing one node.

key_findings.finding: Response bias tests show no evident bias by region or EU accession date, but the authors stress that network data require caution below 100% response.
key_findings.numbers: Region: Pearson chi-square 0.935, p = 0.817 (N = 65). Accession date: chi-square 0.3752, p = 0.540. Response 32 of 65 offices (47%).

key_findings.finding: Theory and method contribution: the authors argue voting interdependence must be modelled at the dyad level with network dependence handled explicitly; the conditional relationship with ideology is central.

limitations: Small network: 32 of 65 offices responded (47%), and the authors say non-response is assumed missing at random (p. 614). A 47% response rate means the network needs caution, and the authors say results below 100% response are less certain (p. 616).
The data are restricted to one committee and one policy area (environment and consumer protection) for one term (p. 613). The authors say generalization is limited (p. 627).

Causality is not resolved: the authors describe a simultaneous, endogenous process between ties and co-voting (pp. 610, 620, 627) and say their empirical tests are compromised by an intractable causality problem (p. 628).

Results are sensitive to specification changes (lagged votes, joint-membership instrument, reverse-causality models) (fn. 81, p. 627). The authors defend the chosen specification but do not show the alternatives.
Hypothesis 2 is not testable: nearly all same-coalition dyads vote together, leaving little variance (p. 625).

Relational measures: connectivity is based on reported contact, which is directed and then symmetrized (p. 617); the connectivity measure is sensitive to specification (fn. 72, p. 620; max-flow alternatives were tried).
The data collection is hard for social network data because staff are reluctant to reveal contacts; the authors say the survey was very specialized and precluded immediate data additions (p. 627).
Missing data and lack of variance on some key terms limit inference (p. 628). Data cannot be shared publicly because of the sensitivity of personal connections (p. 602, fn. on first page).

summary_md:
Ringe, Victor and Gross (BJPS 2013) ask whether legislators' social ties with allies and adversaries relate to how they vote. Their argument is that legislators treat colleagues as sources of cues. A tie to an adversary is useful when the two disagree, because a predictable opponent gives a reliable signal for confirming or revising one's own position.

The data come from staff-reported contacts among the 65 offices on the European Parliament's Environment Committee. The survey ran in 2007 and 32 of the 65 offices responded (47%). Votes are 40 final roll calls on committee bills from 2004 to 2008. The authors model the dyadic co-voting rate with OLS, with a linear mixed model that has crossed random effects for respondent and alter, and with a log-odds mixed model.

For pairs from opposing voting blocs, each extra unit of point connectivity goes with about 10% lower odds of voting together (95% CI 7-13%; n = 1,319 non-unanimous dyads). On the probability scale, predicted co-voting moves from 52% to 44% across ±1 SD of connectivity. Bloc membership dominates (log-odds 2.91), and party adds nothing once bloc is controlled. The allies hypothesis (H2) could not be tested, because 97% of same-bloc dyads always voted together.

The design is cross-sectional and covers one committee in one policy area, with no identification strategy. The authors report that results are sensitive to specification.

The paper matters here for three reasons:
1. Several of Paul's components read a tie, or a cross-party tie, as a positive conduit for alignment. This paper is evidence that contact between opponents is associated with disagreement, not agreement.
2. It supports conditioning network signals on bloc or party, and keeping edge sign. It does not support pooling ties without sign.
3. It shows that dyadic tests need explicit modelling of network dependence, which none of the system's dyad-level checks has.

Every effect here is an association in one EP committee, measured from reported staff contact rather than cosponsorship. It transfers to the US House cosponsorship graph only as a direction to test, not as a calibrated number.

Summary says 97 percent of same-bloc dyads always co-voted; the exact figure is 574 of 594 (96.6 percent). Acceptable rounding, but the denominator should be stated.

gaps_exposed: No dyad-level test in the system models network dependence, such as crossed random effects for both members of a dyad, or QAP and ERGM approaches. This applies to the co-movement tests in stance_dynamics.py, to any future test of whether negative references predict lower cosponsorship, and to cross-party diffusion checks. The paper shows that dyads sharing a member are not independent.

No component conditions the meaning of a tie on whether the pair are expected allies or adversaries (bloc or party pair) before using it as alignment evidence. Neighbour imputation and the 0.4 cross-party diffusion floor both pool or attenuate ties without sign.

No layer treats ties to opponents as information channels, that is, cue-taking from a predictable adversary that confirms one's own position. The system models cross-party ties only as attenuated positive contagion or as zero pressure.

There is no external test of the cross-party sign in the cascade kernel. Neither direction of the cross-party term (positive diffusion at 0.4 + 0.6*sqrt(bpf)) has been checked against US co-voting or cosponsorship outcomes, stratified by party pair.
flags: The paper does not argue for either rejected SNA proposal (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). Its preference for measured contact over cosponsorship proxies must NOT be read as support for dropping cosponsor edges.

The point-connectivity coefficients are heuristic association measures from one EP committee. Under D-025 they must not be restated as closeness, access or introduction probabilities, and influence language should not be used.

The -10% odds figure is a stratum result (opposed-bloc pairs, 1,319 non-unanimous dyads, 40 roll calls 2004-2008). It must not be quoted as a pooled tie effect. The same-bloc hypothesis (H2) was untestable (574 of 594 same-bloc dyads at 100%), so the paper gives no evidence on ties among allies.
The authors report sensitivity to specification (fn. 81) and an unresolved simultaneity problem. Any system use stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it on US data (DE-062).
Paul's position for melange-sna.co-appearance-and-references lists this paper as 'on disk, ink only'. It has now been read in full, so that note is stale.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights centre on the mechanism. Voting is interdependent, ties are strategic choices about information, and adversaries supply cues that update beliefs. He also highlighted the method (multilevel models with crossed random effects for dependence), the use of staff networks as a proxy for office networks, and the headline H1 result. The evidence matches his reading. However, the system has absorbed little of it. Cross-party ties appear only as attenuated positive contagion (cpf_diffusion) or as zero priming pressure (Bakker clamp). No layer uses adversary ties as information channels, and no dyadic test models dependence the way he highlighted. His only listed position cites the paper under co-appearance-and-references as 'ink only'. That is stale: the full paper's main transfer is a caution that unsigned contact is not alignment, plus support for keeping the reference layer signed and stratifying by party pair. The highlight on staff as extensions of their legislators fits the staffer-network premise. But the staff ties in this paper are reported contacts, not concurrent payroll overlap, so it does not validate the overlap edge rule.
